plain.text: Paul has great sorrow and constant anguish for his own people, the Israelites. He says he could almost wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake. They were given so much: adoption as God's children, the glory, the covenants, the law, the temple worship and the promises. The patriarchs are theirs, and from them came the Messiah in his human ancestry.

It is not that God's word has failed. Not everyone descended from Israel is truly Israel. Paul points to God's choice of Isaac over Ishmael, and of Jacob over Esau before they were born, "so that God's purpose in choosing might stand". Is God unjust? Not at all. God told Moses, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy." So it does not depend on human desire or effort, but on God's mercy. Paul uses the picture of a potter who has the right to make different pots from the same clay. God has called people not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, as the prophets Hosea and Isaiah said.

What does this mean? Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith. But Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, did not attain it, because they pursued it as if it came by works rather than by faith. They stumbled over the "stumbling stone" that Scripture speaks of. "Whoever believes in him will never be put to shame."

summary.bigIdea: Paul grieves for his own people and teaches that God's purposes stand, built on his mercy rather than human effort.
points: Paul's deep sorrow for Israel, to whom God gave so much.
God's choosing depends on his mercy: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy."
Righteousness comes by faith, and whoever believes will not be put to shame.
summary.reflection: Paul loved his people so much it hurt. Who do you care about deeply and pray for?
